newsitem.title: MEXICO: Crackdown charged after Mexico rebel clash.
newsitem.headline: Crackdown charged after Mexico rebel clash.

text.p: Mexico's main left-wing party charged on Monday that several of its members had been arrested following a clash last weekend between the military and Marxist guerrillas.

The Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) said at least three of its rural leaders and four peasants who support the PRD had been held since Saturday, when rebels and army troops fought in the southwestern state of Guerrero.
"This could signal a general repression," Ramon Sosamontes, a federal deputy for the PRD, told a news conference. The men were detained in the Chilapa municipality where the battle occured.

Two army troops and two guerrillas died in the firefight between troops and rebels, members of the self-styled Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR). At least three army doctors were also injured in the clash, the military said.
"The government is trying to make it seem as if we are all the same, in spite of the fact that we have said clearly that we are not in agreement with the methods of the EPR," Sosamontes said.
The clash was the first reported this year between the military and the EPR, which sprang up in June 1996 calling for a Marxist popular uprising to overthrow the government.
Since a series of deadly attacks last year, the rebels lapsed into relative inactivity this year, carrying out peaceful acts of propaganda to build support.
Critics of the government say authorities have taken advantage of the attacks to crack down on political dissidents and peasant rights activists.
President Ernesto Zedillo's government has mounted an intense military operation in the mountainous region of Guerrero and other central and southern Mexican states to hunt down the guerrillas.
Municipal officials in Chilapa said the clash left eight soldiers wounded.
Municipal union spokesman Francisco Tacuba told local media the eight wounded were moved to a military hospital in Chilpancingo, the state capital.
A few weeks ago, EPR leaders warned reporters that armed conflict was "imminent" because of what they termed continuing hostilities by the government.
